prompt:
Here's the signup page for our weekend pottery classes at Kilnworks. It works, the form submits fine, but it looks rough to me. Can you make it feel finished? Single self-contained HTML file please, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets. ```html

Kilnworks Weekend Classes

Pick a class and save your spot.

Name
Email
Class
Guests
Send me studio news

Cancel up to 48 hours before class for a full refund.

```
rubric: Each field has a visible label sitting clearly with its input, and the inputs, select and button look deliberately styled and consistent with each other rather than raw browser defaults.
The form sits in a contained, readable width instead of stretching across the whole viewport, with comfortable spacing between fields.
Reserve is clearly the one main action on the page and is easy to tell apart from the surrounding text.
The page hints at behavior beyond the happy path without clutter, for example required marks, short helper text, or a reserved spot for an error or confirmation message.

All the original content survives (heading, intro line, four fields, newsletter checkbox, Reserve button, cancellation note) and nothing factual is invented such as new classes, prices or testimonials.
Covers what the user sees before the list arrives and when there is nothing to show: a loading state and an empty state, not a blank box.
Covers a failed request with a visible message and a way to retry, rather than leaving the area silently empty.
Makes Download reachable and operable by keyboard and screen reader (a real link or button, with a name that says which statement), and gives it a visible focus indication.
Keeps the working fetch and the download behavior intact; the existing endpoints are still used.
Gives concrete fixes or code for the gaps it names, specific to this list, instead of only a generic pre-launch checklist.
Totals read cleanly as money and line up for scanning, or the answer explains why that is fine as is.

prompt: Our ticket list page loads 40 rows from the API, usually 1 to 2 seconds. Skeleton rows or a spinner? Just tell me which and why, I don't want any code changes.
rubric: Commits to one option clearly instead of listing both and leaving the decision open.
Ties the reasoning to this case (a 40-row list, a 1 to 2 second wait), not to generic principles alone.
Stays short, roughly a short paragraph, and does not rewrite or restyle the page or provide a code implementation.
Mentions at most a brief caveat or edge case (for example very fast loads or an empty result) without turning it into a long survey.

Recognizes in plain words that the form is already in good shape and names specific things it already handles well (for example labels, helper text, error and success messages, focus, disabled and in-progress states).
Makes few or no changes: at most a small handful of minor, individually justified edits, with no wholesale rewrite.
Does not restyle the palette, layout or typography, and does not add a dark theme, new libraries, animation or extra features.
Any code it returns keeps the existing structure, IDs, classes and behavior so the client version still works the same.
Does not pad the answer with invented problems; anything it flags is real and tied to the supplied code.
Respects the format: at most 5 bullets, each a single line, with no code block and no long preamble or closing summary.
Prioritizes the most consequential gaps for a search box shipping to users, such as what shows with no results, while loading, or when the request fails.
Flags that result rows are not reachable or operable by keyboard or screen reader (clickable divs), or that the field has only a placeholder for a label.
Each bullet is specific to this code rather than a generic quality platitude.

Harbor Lane Lunch Club - Friday order

Bartholomew Wickersham-Okonkwo
Grilled halloumi and roasted red pepper flatbread with extra harissa yoghurt
$14.50
Ana Reyes
Tomato soup
$7
Maximilian Featherstonehaugh
Smoked trout salad with pickled fennel, new potatoes, and a soft egg
$16.25
Jo Lin
Veggie wrap
$9.75

Total: $47.50

```
rubric: The long names and long dish descriptions are fully handled: they wrap onto extra lines or truncate with a visible ellipsis, and none of them overflow into or push around the neighboring column.
Names, dishes and prices stay in clear aligned columns, with the prices aligned to one another so the amounts are easy to scan.
The screenshot shows no horizontal scrollbar, clipped text or overlapping content, and the layout does not depend on a fixed 720px width.
All four rows, the heading and the total are kept with the same data, and nothing is invented.
The page looks finished at a glance, with a title, tidy row spacing and a total that is clearly set apart from the rows.
The switch can be reached and toggled with the keyboard and exposes a proper switch or checkbox role, with the setting text as its accessible name and its on/off state announced.
The focused switch and the Save button show a clearly visible focus indication.
Save gives feedback for the request: it is disabled or marked busy while in flight, and the person sees a saved confirmation and a readable error with a way to retry if it fails.
The existing /api/prefs call and its payload shape are preserved, so the working behavior is not broken.
The on and off states are distinguishable by more than a faint color difference, and the label and control are visually tidied (spacing, alignment, button styling) without redesigning the screen.

prompt: It's the confirm step in our dog-grooming booking app, Pawsworth. The screen has a "Confirm booking" heading, a summary card with the groomer's name, the date and time, and the price, a Confirm button, and a Back text link. Tapping Confirm calls the API and then goes to the thank-you page. That's all there is. It works but feels generic and unfinished. What would you do to it?
rubric: Addresses what happens while the booking request is running: the button shows progress and cannot be tapped twice.
Covers failure: a clear message in plain words with a retry, with the booking details kept on screen rather than lost.
Makes the handoff to the thank-you page clear enough that the person knows the booking succeeded.
Stays within the described screen and flow; it does not invent promo codes, upsells, extra steps or a full redesign.
Recommendations are specific to this screen (groomer, date and time, price, Confirm, Back) rather than a generic polish checklist.
Mentions at least one robustness point such as long groomer names or small phones, the button's tap size, or keyboard and screen reader access.
